name: Bentonite / clay mask

lead: A bentonite mask is a rinse-off paste made from an absorbent volcanic-ash clay. People with oily or congested skin use it to soak up surface oil and get a less shiny, cleaner-looking face.

Bentonite particles are flat with a large surface area and swell in water, so they adsorb liquids and oils. Users attribute the mattifying effect to this, and it lasts until sebum returns. The clay is a well-characterised industrial material, but no clinical trials of clay masks for oil control or acne were found.

paras: People mix the clay with water (sometimes with other liquids) into a paste, apply a layer to the face or body, leave it on until it begins to dry, and rinse off. It is typically used once or a few times a week within a routine that includes moisturizer afterward. The matte effect is visible straight after rinsing.

Bentonite is described as meeting FDA standards for contact with food and drugs, though the FDA has warned about at least one retail bentonite clay product. Clay can leave skin feeling dry or tight, and individual products and skin reactions vary.

angle.text: People with oily or congested skin use wash-off bentonite clay masks to soak up surface oil, leaving a matte, cleaner-looking face. The effect comes from the clay's absorbency; no clinical trials of clay masks were found.

lead: A bentonite clay mask is a wash-off facial or body product whose main ingredient is bentonite, an absorbent clay made mostly of the mineral montmorillonite. People apply it as a paste to soak up skin oil, leaving a matte finish, and use it in routines aimed at oily, congested or blemish-prone skin to make the complexion look cleaner and clearer.[1]

Bentonite is a swelling clay formed largely by the weathering of volcanic ash; its flat, microscopic particles give a large surface area and let it take up several times its dry weight in water, which underlies its use as an absorbent, binder and carrier. It also has many non-cosmetic uses, including drilling fluids, cat litter and wine clarification.[1][2] Reviews of nanoclays describe bentonite and montmorillonite as biocompatible materials with high surface area and ion-exchange capacity studied as drug carriers.[3]

One 2025 randomized trial from Iran tested a bentonite-based facial mask with Alcea sulphurea extract added to an antibiotic in people with moderate acne, and reported lower lesion counts and severity than a placebo mask.[4]

paras: Bentonite is an absorbent, swelling clay formed largely by the weathering of volcanic ash. The two main commercial types are sodium bentonite, which swells more, and calcium bentonite, which is more common.[1]

Its particles are flat and microscopic, giving a large surface area, and it can take up several times its dry weight in water. These properties underlie its use as an absorbent, binder and carrier.[1]

In skincare, bentonite is typically mixed into a paste, applied to the face for a period, and rinsed off. Manufacturers and users describe the intended effect as drawing out oil and leaving a matte finish. Medicinal and dermatologic uses of bentonite are historical: it has served as a bulk laxative and as a base for dermatologic formulations.[1]
Clay is also used as a carrier in modern formulations; a randomized trial of a hyaluronic acid vectorised with clay reported long-term skin hydration and reduced skin brightness.[5]

Bentonite is described as meeting US FDA standards for contact with food and drugs, though the same source notes an FDA warning concerning a particular retail bentonite clay product, indicating that individual consumer products can carry risks.[1]

A 2025 add-on randomized controlled trial in Sari, Iran enrolled 60 people with moderate acne (30 completing per group). Both groups took azithromycin 250 mg; one added a bentonite and Alcea sulphurea mask rooted in Traditional Persian Medicine and the other a placebo mask. At weeks 4 and 8, total lesion count and Acne Severity Index were significantly lower with the active mask (P < 0.001); lesion count fell about 55 percent and severity about 66 percent from baseline by week 8, and 43 percent of the active group were very satisfied versus 3 percent of placebo. No serious side effects were reported.[4] The mask also contained the plant extract, so the result cannot be attributed to bentonite alone.
